implementation_notes: Kotlin's suspend functions are the canonical stackless coroutine: the compiler transforms the body into a continuation-passing state machine, the continuation is passed as the last parameter, and the suspend colour propagates up the call chain (a suspend function calling a suspend function must be suspend). The library provides the discipline around it: coroutineScope bounds children's lifetimes and cancels them on failure, withContext switches the dispatcher, Flow for streams, and Dispatchers.IO for blocking work. The performance rule that matters: a suspend call that returns without actually suspending (a fast path) is not free - it still allocates the state machine box unless the compiler elides it - so a suspend function called in a tight loop with no real suspension is a measurable cost. launch (fire and forget) inside a scope is safe; GlobalScope.launch is a leak.
idiom_name: suspend functions (compiler CPS state machine) with coroutineScope/withContext/Flow; Dispatchers.IO for blocking
pitfalls: runBlocking blocks a thread; use it only in main() and tests, never on a server or UI thread.
Blocking a Dispatchers.IO thread (a synchronous read or a Mutex held across a delay) occupies the pool and can starve it under load.
Catching CancellationException broadly swallows cancellation and breaks structured concurrency.
withContext(Dispatchers.IO) for blocking I/O, never for CPU-bound work - the IO pool is sized for blocking calls and CPU work starves it.
Holding a thread-local or a lock across a suspension can deadlock, since the coroutine may resume on a different thread.
A suspend function that never actually suspends still has state-machine overhead - do not make a hot loop suspend for nothing.
